models.purpose: Turn the three components of a data-and-analytics system into twelve indicators, each scaled so that one is best.
models.summary: People gives innovation rate, working efficiency and working quality. Technology gives schedule accuracy, cost accuracy, robustness and data-process capability. Process gives data-process efficiency, data security, data accuracy, data-and-cost saving rate and data quality. Nine of them are written as closed formulas; data security and data quality are borrowed and only normalized.

equation_status.reason: Nine indicators are written as displayed formulas; the remaining three are borrowed and only normalized.

objectives: Produce one number per indicator with one as the best value.
constraints: The innovation rate and both throughput indicators are capped at one.
The working-efficiency score uses only the overrun, never the underrun.

details: The indicators are static ratios, not a dynamic system.
Several indicators are truncated at one by a minimum with one.

parameter_estimation.method: The benchmarks and the difficulty coefficient are treated as given; no estimation procedure is stated.

steps: Compute each ratio from its inputs.
Apply the cap or the penalty written in the formula.

assumptions: The data used to compute the indicators is precise because it comes from official sources.
A gap is equally costly once the difficulty coefficient is fixed.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: No data-and-analytics system is actually scored, so none of the nine formulas is evaluated on data.

validation_refs: The indicators are required to be SMART, with measurability stressed.
strengths: Every indicator is forced onto a common scale with one as best.
The formulas are short enough to audit by hand.
limitations: Equation (2) lets the better of the two skills be ignored entirely.
Equation (5) has no absolute value, so an underestimate scores above one and an overestimate can go negative.
Equation (8) is named DPC, then DPE, then DC in the prose.
missing_details: The three borrowed indicators, data security and data quality, are never written as formulas.
No value is given for the difficulty coefficient.

models.purpose: Weight the indicators by mixing entropy weights with analytic-hierarchy weights, then fold the weighted scores into one maturity score and a level.
models.summary: A fuzzy synthetic evaluation builds a score from expert grades. Separately, entropy weights and hierarchy weights are computed per component and mixed with four fifths on the entropy side. The three component scores are averaged, the two methods are mixed again at the same four-fifths ratio, and the result is read against five maturity bands.

equation_status.reason: The weighting, the two scores and the final mix are all displayed.

objectives: Give the objective method four fifths of the weight because the indicators are measurable.
Place the final score on one of five maturity levels.
constraints: The hierarchy share is fixed at one fifth.
The five bands are Initial below 0.2, Repeatable to 0.4, Defined to 0.6, Managed to 0.8, Optimizing to 1.0.

details: The maturity bands partition the unit interval, except that Defined and Managed are both written as opening at 0.4.

parameter_estimation.method: The mixing coefficient is chosen by the authors on the ground that entropy is more objective; no sensitivity over it is shown.

steps: Compute the entropy and the entropy weights.
Average the component scores and mix with the fuzzy score.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: The hierarchy weights are reported as numbers, but the pairwise comparisons behind them are not shown.

assumptions: The experts are equally professional, so no expert is weighted above another.
Equal importance of the three components is defended by the harm of losing any one of them.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: Entropy weights need several objects, but the paper never says what those objects are, and no system is scored end to end.

validation_refs: The final weights are drawn as three donut charts.
models.computational_cost: One entropy pass over an undisclosed matrix plus one hierarchy pass.
strengths: The mix is stated as a number rather than left verbal.
The objective method is given the larger share for a stated reason.
limitations: The reported weight vectors do not all sum to one.
Equation (13) prints Z_m while the prose calls the score Z_F.
Equation (17) uses n where the prose says the number of indicators is m.
Defined and Managed both open at 0.4, so the bands overlap.
missing_details: The objects the entropy is computed over are never identified.
The pairwise comparison matrices for the hierarchy weights are not shown.

models.purpose: Lift the maturity score to the optimizing band at minimum difficulty, then rescale the three component weights for a firm of a different size.
models.summary: The current state is a vector of three component scores. A step is added so the average reaches 0.8, and the step of least difficulty is wanted. Separately, demand for each component is read off a fitted function of firm size and turned back into weights.

equation_status.reason: The objective, the constraint and the rescaling are all displayed.

objectives: Reach an average component score of 0.8 at the smallest difficulty.
constraints: Each component score stays at most one.
The difficulty components are positive and sum to one.

details: The current score vector is the starting point of the step.
The target is a surface, not an equilibrium.

parameter_estimation.method: The difficulty direction is never given a value. The demand curves are fitted to seaport berth counts, with reported coefficients of determination 0.9758 and 0.9731.

steps: State the linear objective and the surface constraint.
No solution procedure is given and no optimal step is reported.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: None stated; the program is linear but is not solved.

assumptions: Reaching the optimizing band is the only improvement worth modelling.
Demand for a component varies smoothly with firm size.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The two demand curves are fitted and cross at one reported point, but the optimization itself is never solved and the difficulty vector is never valued.

validation_refs: Figure 9 shows the two fitted curves and their crossing.
Figure 3 draws the step and the difficulty direction.
models.computational_cost: A three-variable linear program, unsolved, plus two quadratic fits.
strengths: The upgrade is drawn, so the trade-off between components is visible.
The rescaling lets the same model serve firms of different size.
limitations: Improvement inside a maturity level is conceded to be impossible in this model.
The relation between process and scale is conceded to resist quantification.
Equation (23) writes v_i where the prose says k_i.
missing_details: No value is ever given for the difficulty vector.
No optimal step is computed for any starting score.

dependency_edges.handoff: The twelve indicators supply the columns that the entropy and the hierarchy weight.
The mixed component weights and the final score fix the current vector that the optimization pushes to the surface.
